name: Adipotide

lead: Adipotide is an experimental peptide designed to destroy the blood vessels that feed white fat. Obese monkeys lost weight in a 2011 study.
A later comment suggested reduced eating could explain part of the effect. No human results exist.

paras: It binds prohibitin on fat blood vessels and triggers cell death in them, starving fat tissue.
Human safety is unknown, and it is not approved. Clinical development was reported discontinued.

studies.title: Comment on "a peptidomimetic targeting white fat causes weight loss and improved insulin resistance in obese monkeys".

lead: Adipotide (also called prohibitin-targeting peptide 1, FTPP or TP01) is an experimental peptidomimetic designed to bind prohibitin and annexin A2 on the blood vessels feeding white fat, inducing the death of those vessels and, in turn, fat tissue.[1]

In a 2011 study in obese rhesus monkeys, treatment reduced body weight and improved insulin resistance.[2] A 2012 published comment proposed the weight loss might instead reflect reduced food intake.[3] Wikipedia lists its status as investigational, with clinical development discontinued as of 2019.[1] No human trial results are published.

paras: The compound fuses a fat-vasculature-homing motif to a proapoptotic peptide, aiming to damage vessels supplying white adipose tissue.[2][1] Nanoparticle approaches targeting the same marker, prohibitin, have been compared with the peptide conjugate in mice.[4]

The 2011 Science Translational Medicine study reported weight loss and improved insulin resistance in obese monkeys.[2] A commentary in the same journal argued that the effect could reflect a direct reduction in food consumption.[3]
No studies found. Published work is limited to animal studies.
Adipotide is sold online as a research peptide and is not an approved medicine. It is discussed in fat-loss communities, though no human data support its use.

timeline.event: Comment questions the mechanism of weight loss.[3]
